Psychologically, all that remains is the touching expectation expressed in a Baroque poem, J. Ch. Günther’s “Aria of Consolation”:
At last, at last envy can die, At last Herod too can die, At last David’s shepherd’s cloak Can dye its hem in purple. At last time makes Saul Too weak and tired to persecute.

I see with horror that the standpoint of the just war destroys every such hope. It instantly sweeps away every argument—whether the principle that one may not contradict one’s own previous conduct, or an appeal to specific or general provisions of the laws of land warfare. And in the victor it immediately suffocates every impulse toward reciprocal thinking. That is why I regret that Rolf Stödter dismisses this subject very briefly in his otherwise thorough book (p. 107).
C. M. O. van Nispen tot Sevenaer (The Hague, 1946) confirms my fears.
Barandon’s Hamburg radio lecture on the Bochum dismantling trials of February 1949, meanwhile, shows that even an old and cautious diplomat can become tactless through sheer excess of caution.
Until now, Germans have generally been able to distinguish only between I and non-I, not between friend and enemy.
The result was that they confused every non-I with the enemy.
Then, once they realized how absurd that was, they believed they could put everything right again with a “kiss for the whole world.”
How could the precious salt of self-irony ever flourish under such conditions?
(To Otto Veit, thanking him for sending the speeches of 29 December 1948:)
But the I is not the friend. And the non-I is not the enemy. This is not about epistemology or metaphysics. It is about concentrations of power within which one has to hold one’s ground.
“One”—yes, one, you dreary pedant, with your cheap, smug, pseudo-philosophical criticism of the word one!
Deify the body and embody God!
I see in you the God Whom shuddering I recognized, To whom my devotion belongs!
The beautiful body and the healthy animal: the new God. And all of it standing in the foreground before the great machine.

I would like to identify the point at which the legal scholar’s normative concept of law and the natural scientist’s causal concept of law meet again deep below the surface, after neo-Kantianism in Germany had separated them so sharply.
The law in which Rousseau and Michelet believed was incapable of such divisions.
What a falsification of the myth of law and of the lawgiver.
The Législateur is powerless, en quelque façon nul—in a certain sense, nothing—just as only science can still be powerless today.
We are all en quelque façon nul.
Only science today is still capable of pure powerlessness and therefore of purity.

Even Kurt Hiller’s agitated flailing around over the word “enemy”—in his article against Paetel in Die Weltbühne of 4 October 1932—gives some sense of the wonderful dialectic of which the concept of the “enemy” is capable and in need.
Age grants me, as a touching compensation for physical and social misfortune, the most beautiful migrations of cranes—not only of the spirit but also of the imagination.

Unfortunately, it is precisely honest and helpful people who underestimate the extent and intensity of the extra-legal persecution being carried out against me by some of my older colleagues. It would be wrong of me to bring people who want to help me into contact with the existential hatred and will to destroy that drive those persecutors.

“That immediate giving of laws is therefore the tyrannical outrage that turns arbitrary will into law and ethical life into obedience to it—obedience to laws that are merely laws and not at the same time commandments.”
“As a particular law, the law has an accidental content.”
(Compare the remarks on Hegel of 22 February 1949 and 14 December 1948.)
Hegel’s double face is the authentic German face.
His double meaning is the German way of making sense.
“The men of the German National Assembly in Frankfurt wanted to found a Reich whose very existence would have been equivalent to a European revolution.”
Instead, another Reich was founded whose very existence became equivalent to a world revolution.
The poor little men in Bonn, meanwhile, are straining themselves to found a non-Reich whose existence is supposed to mean the avoidance of every change to the status quo.

In other words: the preservation of a status quo that has long since become chaotic—so chaotic that even calling it a status already sounds like a bad joke. They would like, after the fact, to pretend that none of the possibilities that once existed were ever real.
I wonder whether there is a single reader of my Donoso essay who clearly understands all this, or even dimly senses it.
Oberheid, who read the essay, cannot understand my language.
Worse: the moment he hears my language, he can no longer understand anything at all.
Wilhelm Schmitz ought to be given the essay to read.
Even so, it is good that the Donoso essay now exists in print in German. It had to be deposited in the asylum offered by the Dominicans.
Not everyone has the right to offer me asylum.
One genuine asylum today means more than many written constitutions.
The state was the present God for them. For the Prussians, that is. They took an anti-theological French experience with theological seriousness.
The state was the Prussian sacrament.
Still better than the cinema or a party rally.
Still better than a meeting of the UN or UNESCO.

No one will ever call those things the present God. That would not even make a good bad joke. But the Prussian sacrament was also better than the humanitarian one—better by exactly the degree to which a tragedy by Kleist is greater than one by Goethe.
A profoundly German invention: resistance through cooperation.
“For war presupposes in those who make it, if not equality of strength, then at least the belief in such equality; from this arises in each side the desire and hope of defeating the other.”
In the state of nature, everyone can possess that hope.

So writes d’Alembert in the Analysis of The Spirit of the Laws, Serving as a Continuation of the Éloge of M. de Montesquieu—the introduction to the five-volume Montesquieu edition, Paris, Chez Jean-François Bastien, 1788.

Today they no longer have the slightest idea what they are doing when they say that fighting has become meaningless because weapons have become so unequal. And that is supposed to amount to the outlawing of war?
D’Alembert, in this Analysis, still follows Thomas Hobbes completely.
Very fine, Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws, XII, chapter 5:
“One must be extremely cautious in the prosecution of magic and heresy.”
“Tyranny can abuse even the horror that one ought to feel toward it.”
I see: tyranny loves to exploit that horror.
Moral outrage—or moral rearmament—is now nothing more than a pretext for confiscating property, creating jobs and salaried civil-service posts, and exterminating the enemy.
The crime against humanity is simply the new edition of the old crime against nature.

If we keep this level of readability, I think we have the right voice for the rest of Glossarium: unmistakably Schmitt, but with almost none of the unnecessary friction that a modern reader would otherwise feel.
What a flood of throwbacks to the past—this liberation of Germany through the psychoses of 1945!
Do not forget the striking parallel between foreign and domestic affairs throughout the whole development from 1919 to 1939.

Abroad: France and England refused the Weimar democratic government even the smallest amount of rearmament. Schleicher had to make way for Hitler when he tried to increase the Reichswehr from 100,000 to 300,000 men. Yet afterward, those same powers allowed Hitler to rearm without restraint from 1935 onward.

At home: from 1925 onward, the Reichstag refused to grant emergency powers to governments that depended on its own confidence. It preferred to let the Reich President issue emergency decrees under Article 48. But then this same Reichstag suddenly gave Hitler the insane powers granted by the law of 24 March 1933.

What does this mean? That is the only important question, and the starting point for any honest answer. It means many things. Among them, that figures like Hitler are genuine executors: collectors of unpaid debts; releasers of forces that have been dammed up too long; agents who finally carry out ideals whose realization has long been overdue.
You moral people, filled with outrage: one day you will be taken at your word.

For the first time, establish jurisprudence as an independent intellectual authority, instead of what it has been until now: a function of political, social, or professional developments and interests.
Justice is not a profession, a subject, a specialty, or a function.
Today, the administration of justice means deciding disputes—in other words, maintaining public safety and order through the police.
The claim that justice itself can be cultivated as the profession and official duty of ordinary human beings is a lie.
Perhaps one could imagine an order whose members were prepared to accept martyrdom for justice. But they would not be lawyers.
What exactly are you doing in Plettenberg?
I am making the transition from existence to essence.
I am de-existentializing myself and my being.
